newsitem.title: USA: Productivity rises at slower pace in third quarter.
newsitem.headline: Productivity rises at slower pace in third quarter.

text.p: U.S. business productivity rose at a slower pace in the third quarter, the government said Thursday, but the manufacturing sector staged its best performance in two-and-a-half years.
The Labour Department reported that productivity outside of the agricultural sector rose just 0.2 percent in the third quarter after rising 0.5 percent in the previous quarter.
Still, the gains were better than expected given the economy's recent, sharp slowdown.
The government reported last week that the nation's gross domestic product in the third quarter grew at less than half the robust pace of the previous quarter.
Wall Street economists on average had predicted that non-farm productivity would fall 0.1 percent in the third quarter.

"Given that third-quarter GDP was somewhat anaemic I guess you'd expect productivity to be doing badly," said Bill Cheney, chief economist at John Hancock Financial Services in Boston. "At least it's not a negative number."

By contrast, the manufacturing sector roared ahead, with productivity jumping 6.3 percent, the biggest gain since the first quarter of 1994, when it rose 6.7 percent. Manufacturing accounts for roughly 18 percent of the nation's business sector jobs.
Some economists expect the latest slowdown in overall business productivity to prove temporary.

"This is by no means a reflection of labour not working hard or business not giving labour the right tools," said Irwin Kellner, chief economist for Chase Manhattan's regional bank. "It's clearly a reflection of the slowdown in economic growth."
Kellner maintained that businesses were not able to curtail the growth in labour hours as quickly as they slowed output.
"This is a one-quarter phenomenon," Kellner predicted. "It doesn't mean profit margins are going to be pinched or that there will be (upward) pressure on prices."

Non-farm productivity data provide a reading on the efficiency of business by measuring the amount of goods and services produced per hour by all workers. Healthy growth in productivity allows wages to rise proportionately without accelerating inflation.
But some economists fear the third-quarter assessment of labour costs could prove worrisome for the inflation outlook.
Unit labour costs, which make up two-thirds of businesses' production costs, rose at a 3.7 percent rate in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent in the previous month.
"That could be critical in keeping inflation a concern in the markets," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis.
Financial markets have been watching closely for signs of labour market tightness amid concern that higher labour costs could trigger inflation and prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.

But the Fed may pay closer attention to the strong efficiency gains in manufacturing, given the government's difficulty in measuring service sector productivity, according to David Orr, chief capital markets economist at First Union.
In another report, the department said the number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell in the latest week.
The Labour Department said 331,000 people filed first-time claims for unemployment insurance payments in the week ended Nov. 2, compared with 342,000 claims made in the previous week.
